job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My days start loud. I live with my parents, my two brothers and my aunt in a terraced house in Bradford, and breakfast is a crowd. I finished a computing degree in July, web and cloud systems, with a pass. My final project was a rota website for a food bank run by our mosque, and about thirty volunteers use it every week. Then I'm at the laptop upstairs, working with an AI assistant on a small site for my cousin's cake business and sending applications.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you learn from running something for thirty volunteers?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad owns a small grocery shop and he's very much a believer in working for yourself. My mum is the one who actually runs everything. I did no internships because I spent summers in the shop, and I used to think that didn't count, but it taught me how customers behave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I'd guess. The tools help, but nothing's magic, and the people who make things still win. I'd post about my cousin's cake site, because real projects are better than opinions. At home I'd say good, nothing to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan is simple. Get a first job, keep freelancing, build a name. I've got plenty of openings in the area and a family that will back me for as long as it takes. I'm not frightened, but I'm a bit impatient, because I'd like to be paying my way by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send 20 applications a month to digital agencies, and I'd keep working on three small client sites at once. I'd ask my cousin and the food bank manager for short written testimonials. I'd also use the AI tools even more, for writing boring code and checking my own. I'd start saving 150 a month toward a laptop that doesn't overheat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and busy. I'm someone who feels better when I have three things on the go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like to be paying your way by Christmas. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad never says it, but he has opinions about people who sit around. I want to show him I'm building something. My dad would say a business isn't a hobby. I invoice every client properly, even my cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the AI help with the cake site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It writes the first draft of the code and the product descriptions. I rewrite most of it, and I test everything on my phone. My cousin said the descriptions sounded like me, which was funny, because I changed half of it.

say: I'd say the tools help, but **real projects** beat opinions.
At home I'd say, good, nothing to fix.
think: My plan is simple: **first job**, keep freelancing, build a name.
I'm not frightened, but I'm **impatient** to pay my way.
do: Send **20 applications a month** to digital agencies while running three client sites.
Collect **testimonials** and save 150 a month toward a better laptop.
feel: **Calm and busy**; I feel better with three things on the go.

fieldNote: Her dad's **business** outlook shapes how she treats freelancing.

steps.text: Send 20 applications a month to digital agencies
Run three small client websites and invoice each one properly
Use an AI assistant for first drafts of code and descriptions
Save 150 a month toward a better laptop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and fast, and the people who learn it first will do well. I'd also say families and mosques and groups like ours should help people get ready, not leave them alone. I'd say it at the food bank and online, with examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the junior coding jobs I'm applying for shrink. Agencies that hired five juniors will hire two and expect each to use AI for everything. But I already work that way, so I think I'm in a decent spot. The ones in trouble are people who never touched the tools and wait to be told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after small businesses directly, since agencies might cut back. Websites, ordering systems, simple automations for shops like my dad's. I'd also join an online freelancer group and a local business network. I'd price per project, and learn a payments tool so clients can pay online. And I'd use my family network of shopkeepers, because they all need help and they trust me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also quite excited. I feel like something could open up for people who move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said groups like yours should help people get ready. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A free evening class at the mosque hall where someone who knows the tools sits with people. Not a lecture, just a person at a laptop. My aunt would be the first to come, she keeps asking me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Hamza, who's doing a business course and thinks AI is a fad. And older people at the shop who can't read the new forms. I'd be the family's IT person, which I already am.

say: I'd say groups like ours should **help people get ready**, not leave them alone.
I'd say it at the food bank and online, with examples.
think: Junior coding jobs shrink, but I already **work with AI** daily.
People in trouble are those who never touched the tools and **wait to be told**.
do: Pitch **websites and ordering systems** straight to small shops, starting with my dad's.
Join a **freelancer group** and learn a payments tool so clients pay online.
feel: **Uneasy**, but excited that something may open for people who move first.

fieldNote: Moves **first**, as her adaptive profile suggests.

Worries about her brother **Hamza**, who calls AI a fad.

steps.text: Pitch websites and ordering systems to shops in my dad's street
Build a simple stock and orders automation for my dad's grocery
Run a free evening class on AI tools at the mosque hall
Learn a payments tool so clients can pay online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot to take in, and we need to look after one another. I'd say families need to talk now and decide who earns, who saves, who helps. In the community I'd ask the elders to host a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's frightening, and exciting in an unhelpful way. If AI can do almost any thinking job by 2028, my freelance work is competing with a free tool. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so my dad's shop and a mechanic cousin would last longer. I'd be the odd one in the family whose job disappears first, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd help my dad automate his shop's ordering and stock, then charge other shopkeepers for the same. I'd tell the family we're pooling savings for a year, and I'd put mine in with theirs. I'd start learning a hands-on skill, maybe solar installation, because my uncle knows people. And I'd stay close to the AI companies' tools, to see what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thinking about whether my brothers will get a start at all, and whether we'd be okay in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pool savings with the family. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a crisis my family gets organised. My dad would call a meeting after prayers, my mum would put a number on the table, and I'd bring the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hamza and Idris, you need to learn how to use these tools and also a hands-on skill. Don't lean on a degree. I'd say it nicely, but I'd say it more than once.

say: I'd say families must **talk now** about who earns, who saves, who helps.
I'd ask the community elders to host a meeting.
think: My freelance work would compete with a **free tool**.
I'd be the one in the family whose job **disappears first**.

fieldNote: Her answer is **collective**: family savings, family meetings.

steps.text: Automate my dad's shop ordering and sell the setup to other shopkeepers
Pool my savings with the family's for a year
Take a solar installation course through my uncle's contacts
Hold a family meeting after prayers to plan who earns and who saves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something we can work with. I'd tell friends to use it well, build skills, build savings, and look after people around them. I'd say it online as a plan, not a warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel like I have a real chance. In five years I could have a job, a small business and a few clients who rely on me. By 2031 I'd have six years of experience. Robots for hands-on work would be around 2034, so the practical side of tech work would still give me options. I think I'd be more prepared than most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best agency job I can get in six months and keep freelancing on weekends. I'd save about a third of what I earn and buy part of my dad's building or a share in a small flat. I'd keep building tools with AI, and start a small company with my cousin, since our skills fit. And I'd help my brothers pick a course that isn't just a degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and ambitious. I'd feel like I was choosing my road, which I haven't in the last six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a share in a small flat. Why property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my parents did it, and it's what they know. My dad says rent is a wall you pay for twice. I'd keep half in a savings account, though, because I've seen property get stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the company with your cousin do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cakes online, to start, then websites for other food sellers. She makes the product, I make the shop. It's small, but she has customers who love her, and I have the tech.

I'd frame it online as a plan, not a warning.
think: I'd have a **real chance** with a job, a small business and clients.
I'd be more prepared than most because of my **six years** of experience.

steps.text: Take the best agency job offered within six months
Start an online shop and web service with my cousin
Save a third of my earnings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so I'd tell friends to build something while they can. I'd say we should check on each other at family gatherings. I'd probably post about learning to code at any age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty positive. A decade is time to have a career, a small company, maybe a family. By 2036 I'd be thirty-three and know how to use the tools better than most people. Robots for hands-on work around 2039 means my brothers have time too. The thing I'd worry about is being comfortable and forgetting to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, save and start the business with my cousin. I'd take a degree top-up in data or cloud security part-time, because those roles still need people who answer for the work. I'd help my parents with their shop, and take on one volunteer project a year, like the food bank rota. And I'd marry in that time, if I find the right person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I think I'd be happy, with ordinary worries, like whether my parents are okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd marry if you find the right person. What would that mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family would want it to happen at a good time, and I'd want my own work in place first. I'd say, give me till twenty-eight. My mum would say, we'll see, and add a list of names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not want to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The food bank project. Thirty volunteers sign up through something I made, and that matters more to me than the invoice. I'd keep one project a year, always.

I'd check on friends at family gatherings.

My worry is being **comfortable** and forgetting to prepare.

Study cloud security part-time over three years
Grow the online shop and web service with my cousin

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It's the one where my family's savings and my freelance work get hit at the same time. What would help is cheap, fast training near home, and tax breaks for small family firms so they can keep hiring the young.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people expect my generation to be glued to our screens and lazy about work. Many of us work in family shops, volunteer and build things at the same time.

headlineQuote: People expect my generation to be glued to our screens and lazy about work. Many of us work in family shops, volunteer and build things at the same time.
portrait: Rosa is **23**, a web and cloud computing graduate with a pass, in a crowded Bradford family house.
She uses AI **every day**, rewrites what it gives her, and runs small freelance sites while she applies for jobs.
She is traditional and pro-business, shaped by her father's grocery shop, and backs **family savings** and community help over state aid.
Her mood is calm in most worlds and **anxious** only in 2028, when savings and freelance work could both be hit.
She turns worry into **action** fast: automate her dad's shop, pool family savings, start a business with her cousin.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most because family savings and her freelance work could be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast **training** close to home, and tax breaks so small family firms can keep hiring the young.
